description:
Hi, I'm a GIS analyst and environmental researcher based in Canberra. I work with spatial data on climate and energy issues and have built mapping tools in previous hackathons. I bring spatial analysis, environmental knowledge and clear storytelling for the final pitch.

I'm looking for teammates with Python or data science skills (especially satellite data), web or dashboard development, and design or presentation skills. If you care about climate and want to build something useful, join us!
summary:
HORIZON is a web app that tells you whether a lander at any spot near the Moon’s south pole will have sunlight for power and a clear line to Earth for radio. Near the pole the Sun never climbs high and instead circles along the horizon, so a ridge tens of kilometres away can block it for days at a time. The challenge asks for a quick way to compare landing sites and times, and to re-check them whenever schedules change.

You choose a site or enter any coordinates, then set a landing date and hour. HORIZON checks every hour of the mission against NASA LRO laser-altimeter terrain and JPL positions for the Sun and Earth. It returns “Good to land” or “Not good on this date”, shows how long remains before sunset and Earthset, and suggests other days or sites that would work. To make the trade-offs visible, it includes a launch-delay slider, a calendar showing every site on every day, and a 3D view of the real terrain.

HORIZON’s results match NASA Goddard’s south-pole sunlight maps with a correlation of 0.99 across 160 points, and when we replayed India’s Chandrayaan-3 mission, it placed sunset on the same day ISRO put the lander to sleep.
details:
What it does and how it works


HORIZON is a web app for picking landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. You choose a site or type any coordinates between 75°S and the pole, then set a landing date and hour, and HORIZON tells you whether a lander there will have sunlight for solar power and a clear line to Earth for radio. The answer comes as a plain “Good to land” or “Not good on this date”, with meters for sunlight, Earth contact and battery, and a countdown to the next sunset and Earthset. When the answer is no, “Try instead” buttons suggest the nearest day or another site that works.

Near the pole the Sun never climbs high and instead circles just above the horizon, so a ridge tens of kilometres away can block it for days. To handle this, HORIZON traces each site’s skyline in 720 directions out to 300 km across NASA LOLA laser-altimeter terrain, allowing for the Moon’s curvature, then compares that skyline with hourly Sun and Earth positions from JPL’s DE440 ephemeris. From there the browser works out how much of the Sun’s disk clears the skyline, whether Earth is in view, and whether a simple battery lasts through the dark periods.

The main feature is the Slip Matrix, built for the moment a launch is delayed. It checks every site against every landing day from 30 days early to 30 days late, and it updates instantly when you change your mission’s requirements or mast height. The app also has:

  • a 3D model of the real terrain, lit by the Sun at its true position
  • a 360° sky view showing the paths of the Sun and Earth over the skyline
  • side-by-side site comparisons
  • replays of three real landings

Benefits and intended impact


Today, answering “if we land 20 days late, does this site still work?” takes an expert and several tools, and HORIZON answers it on one screen as soon as the schedule slips. We want mission planners, students and the public to see why the south pole is such a hard place to land, and to be able to check any site before committing to it. Replaying India’s Chandrayaan-3 puts sunset at its landing site on 4 Sep 2023, the same day ISRO put the lander to sleep. Our next steps are the north pole, sunlit rover routes and modelling lander tilt.

Tools, languages and software

  • Precomputation: Python, with NumPy, SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF SPICE) and Pillow
    • NASA LRO LOLA polar terrain maps
    • JPL DE440 ephemeris
    • JPL Horizons and NASA Goddard illumination maps (for validation)
    • USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (for feature locations)
  • Hardware: none, since this is a software-only project

How it’s creative

  • Besides finding a good site, it answers the question teams actually face: what happens when the launch slips?
  • It replays real missions (Chandrayaan-3, IM-1 and IM-2) and sets its predictions beside what actually happened.
  • The 3D “Stand on the Moon” view places you at the lander’s mast height and stretches the picture vertically so that skylines only 1 to 3° high become visible, while keeping which features hide behind which exactly as they are in the data.
  • You can pick any spot as well as the preset sites, and the browser traces a new skyline for it in about a second.

Factors I considered

  • Accuracy:
    • Long-run sunlight and Earth visibility match NASA Goddard’s polar illumination maps at 160 locations (correlation 0.99).
    • Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.000025°.
    • Terrain heights match NASA LROC’s published elevations to within 2 to 14 m.
    • terrain detail is 40 m or coarser, so it misses boulders and small craters
    • site coordinates are for illustration only
    • the battery model is deliberately simple
  • Sharing: a link saves the exact plan, so it can be passed to someone else.
